subject: Geography
source: Gap-fill against AQA GCSE Geography 8035 specification

lessons.unit: Unit 3.2.3.1: Resource management (3.2.3 The challenge of resource management) - compulsory
lessons.title: The changing energy mix: from fossil fuels to renewables
lessons.bigQuestion: How has where our energy comes from changed, and why?
objectives: Describe the changing energy mix of the UK
Explain the decline of fossil fuels and the growth of renewables
Evaluate how far renewables can replace fossil fuels
successCriteria: Most: describe the change in UK energy sources
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship of the Earth for future generations

keywords.def: the proportion of different energy sources used
energy from sources that are replenished, such as wind and solar

teach.heading: What is the energy mix?
bullets: The mix is the share of each source.
UK electricity and total energy are different.
Oil and gas still supply heating and transport.
teach.note: Define energy mix and separate electricity from total energy. For electricity, renewable sources overtook fossil fuels in a recent year (verify the exact year and share). Oil and natural gas are still used for transport and heating. Keep all statistics approximate and flagged for verification. Case-study figures are approximate; verify against current sources before teaching.

teach.heading: The decline of fossil fuels
bullets: Coal supplied most electricity a century ago.
Coal use fell sharply in recent decades.
The last coal-fired power station in the UK closed in 2024.
teach.note: The last UK coal power station, Ratcliffe-on-Soar, closed in September 2024 (verify). Reasons: coal is highly polluting; cheaper gas and renewables; climate policy. North Sea oil and gas production has also declined from its peak, so the UK imports more (verify).

teach.heading: The rise of renewables
bullets: Wind, solar and biomass have grown quickly.
Offshore wind is a large part of UK electricity.
Costs have fallen and the UK has net zero targets.
teach.note: Mention the 2019 law committing to net zero by 2050 (verify). Offshore wind is strong because of high wind speeds around the UK coast. Costs for wind and solar have dropped significantly. Ask why growth is sometimes slow: planning, grid connection, and intermittency.

teach.heading: Reasons for change
teach.note: Organise reasons: economic, environmental and political. Link to 'energy security' from previous lessons. Use a table; pupils annotate with an example for each.

head: Type
Reason
rows: Reduce carbon emissions and air pollution
Wind and solar costs have fallen

teach.heading: Worked example
teach.note: Model describing a trend then explaining. Teach: 'Describe' uses figures from the source; 'Explain' uses linking words.

model.problem: Explain why the UK's energy mix has changed. (4 marks)
steps: Coal use fell because it is polluting and a major source of carbon dioxide
Climate policy and net zero targets encourage cleaner sources
Costs of wind and solar have fallen, making them competitive
Together these changes reduced reliance on fossil fuels
model.answer: Reasons linked in a chain, with at least one developed

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. A is energy security. C is a fossil fuel. D is incorrect.

check.q: Which is the best description of 'energy mix'?
options: The proportion of different energy sources used
check.why: Energy mix means the share of each energy source in a country's supply.

practice: Sort into fossil fuel or renewable: gas, solar, coal, offshore wind, oil, biomass.
Give two reasons why UK coal use has fallen.
independent: Core: Describe how the UK's energy mix has changed. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain why fossil fuel use has declined while renewables have grown. (6 marks)
Stretch: 'The UK can rely entirely on renewable energy.' Evaluate this view. (9 marks)
exit: Return to the big question: how and why has it changed?
lessons.homework: Find a UK energy mix chart, note two changes over time and one reason for each. Mark any figure to verify.
lessons.send: SEND: sorting cards and a labelled chart. EAL: key words with pictures. Stretch: compare the UK mix with another country.

lessons.title: Using sources in issue evaluation: maps, graphs, statistics, photographs, satellite images and statements
lessons.bigQuestion: How can different sources support a decision, and how reliable are they?
objectives: Identify the types of source used in the issue evaluation booklet
Extract and use evidence from each type
Judge the usefulness and bias of sources
successCriteria: All: name source types and say what they show
Most: use evidence from three source types
Some: evaluate bias, reliability and limits of sources
lessons.smsc: Moral: truthful use of evidence and fairness to stakeholders

keywords.def: a person or group affected by a decision
facts or information supporting a view
a picture of Earth's surface from space

starter: Name two sources you could use in a geographical enquiry.

teach.heading: The source types
teach.note: Explain that the issue evaluation booklet contains a range of sources and the exam asks you to use them to reach a justified decision. The topic changes each year, so we practice with an invented example here: a proposal for a new flood barrier in a town. All numbers in this lesson are illustrative.

teach.heading: Extracting evidence
bullets: Quote or use a figure from the source.
teach.note: Practice the format: evidence, meaning, link. Example: 'Source C shows 120 homes flooded in 2019, which means the town has a high flood risk, so it supports building the barrier.' Insist on using numbers and names from sources rather than general statements.

teach.heading: Worked example: weighing sources
teach.note: Show how to use two sources with a limitation. Illustrative scenario: a graph shows rising flood events and a stakeholder statement from the council supporting the barrier. The council is a stakeholder with an interest, so it may be biased.

model.problem: Illustrative: a graph shows 3 floods in 2000-2009 and 7 in 2010-2019. A council statement says the barrier is 'essential'. Use the sources to support the barrier and comment on reliability. (4 marks)
steps: Evidence: the graph shows floods rising from 3 to 7 per decade
Meaning: flood risk is increasing, so a barrier is more needed
Link to the decision: supports building the barrier
Reliability: the council may want the barrier to be approved, so its statement may be biased; the graph is more objective

teach.heading: Limits and bias
bullets: Statistics may be averages that hide differences.
Stakeholders argue for their own interests.
teach.note: Ask pupils to pick one source and say one weakness. Sources used together (triangulation) give a stronger case. In the exam, decisions need a reasoned recommendation and an alternative considered.

misconception.wrong: A source is useless if it is biased
misconception.right: Biased sources can still be useful for understanding a view; check them against other evidence

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. A is a weakness of maps. B is the benefit not the weakness. D is not relevant.

check.q: Why should you be cautious about a single stakeholder statement?
options: It may reflect that group's own interests
check.why: Stakeholders may be biased toward their own interests, so check with other sources.

practice: Match each source to one strength and one weakness.
Write an evidence, meaning, link sentence using a statistic.
independent: Core: Name four types of source and say what each shows. (4 marks)
Extend: Use a source of your choice from an example booklet to support a decision. (4 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate how useful the sources are in making a decision. (6 marks)
exit: Which source type is likely to show bias?
Return to the big question: how can sources support a decision?
lessons.homework: Take any news report on a local development and list the types of source it uses and how reliable each is.
lessons.send: SEND: source table with sentence starters. EAL: bilingual glossary. Stretch: rank the sources for reliability and justify.
